body_markdown:
Each fall in Northern Michigan, the weather changes before the leaves do. I know fall is near when I realize I’m working in my shop with the garage doors open for the first time since May, and when a morning commute by motorcycle calls for an extra layer or the heated grips. Fall represents an opportunity to enjoy a small luxury I’ve built into my life, while also forcing me to confront the annoyances that come with a hobby built around old vehicles.


Fall is a word that has a lot of negative connotations, especially as a motorcyclist. I lived my best motorcycling summer this year—though I took the Corvette on[a shakedown drive](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-ls-swap-corvettes-first-drive-went-exactly-as-expected/) , it was the KTM I took on adventures and used to commute to work. I didn’t take it on any particularly impressive trips, but I rode more than I usually do, and that’s a victory.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The impending storage season brings the opportunity to catch up on all the maintenance I deferred during the short riding season, it being my policy never to change a vehicle’s oil when I could be out having fun in some other vehicle. I didn’t really mention the cars above, because this summer I didn’t get a ton of driving in. The Corvette’s LS swap has been progressing swimmingly, but even with steady progress, the car is[on jackstands](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-ls-swapped-corvette-returns-to-jackstands/) more often than it is on the road. (Such is the nature of the project-car beast.)


The other stall in my garage has been occupied with the[1930 Model A Ford](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/3-mistakes-made-while-getting-my-model-a-out-of-storage/) that I love to look at but apparently do not like to do much else with. It got out of the garage twice this summer, and one of those outings was only around the neighborhood. The reality is tough, but also not something I should be complaining about. Having the ability to let the Model A (or any other vehicle) sit for extended periods is a luxury. Vehicles don’t get worse when properly stored—as this Model A always is—and while on hiatus, they always provide opportunities for good daydreaming.


Another reason that I become distracted from regular maintenance is the garage itself. This time of year, the garage is more distracting than normal, because winter, when all of my fun things get locked into this 700-square-foot toybox for the better part of the year, is hauntingly close. It is nearly time for my annual garage reset.


It’s not a huge space, but it’s mine and well equipped for fun projects.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This is the great reshuffling of things to set the proper stage for project season—or, at least, what has historically been project season. This year, I feel as though I spent more time than ever working ** on my junk and less than ever actually driving or using the stuff. Of course, this is the natural ebb and flow of life, but upon reflection, I failed to recognize two things.


The first is that driving is time-consuming, at least comparatively. The biggest luxury of my garage is its location—it is not quite, but almost, attached to my home. If I can find 20 minutes or so, I can walk out to the shop and actually accomplish something. A 20-minute drive, on the other hand, is not actually 20 minutes of driving. (It takes five minutes to get the car out, five minutes to get somewhere I want to drive, then I can only spare a few minutes for actual *fun* driving before I have to turn around, drive back, and put the car away.)


Of course, 20 minutes in the shop is not actually 20 minutes in the shop, but there, I get to spend more of that 20 minutes doing what I actually want to do. The commute from couch to shop is virtually non-existent, and if conditions or opinions change, it takes no time to return. In fact, thanks to a hybrid work schedule that allows me to work from home two days a week, I’ve often used my lunch break to clean a few parts or assemble one little thing on a motorcycle before returning to the desk to finish out the day.


This kind of side area is reserved for motorcycle or “one weekend” projects that come in and out quickly.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The large back bench is for long-term projects and things that require more space and effort.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


It’s not a huge space, but it’s mine and well equipped for fun projects.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The second thing I’ve realized is the way in which my shop space has evolved and changed over the relatively few years I’ve been here. For my wife and me, this medium-sized garage played no small part in the purchase of this home. Since day one, I’ve dreamed of what the garage could be while spending plenty of time to create the best and most functional version of the workspace I currently have. Modular elements like workbenches on wheels help ensure that while my interests and ideas may change, the space will still accommodate whatever I bring in.


The projects in the garage are not the only things that need work. Balancing the storage needs of my garage with the workspace capacity of my shop within one building will always require effort, and I doubt there will ever come a day when I don’t find myself sitting in bed wondering if shuffling a workbench or tool to the other side of the shop will make things easier, more fun, or less dangerous.


Fall is the time of year I work *on* the shop. Winter is the time to work *in* the shop, and summer is the time to do fun things only. I’m learning to embrace each season as if I were a kid again and, after eating chocolate ice cream for dessert for several months, opened the freezer to find a gallon of vanilla. That makes me wonder … if I relocate the garage fridge from the south wall to the west wall, could I open up a small amount of space to make the next motorcycle build or automotive engine-out project just a little easier? That’s an idea …


No, the Corvette’s Dana 44HD differential is not back together yet. But it will be soon, I promise.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Who doesn’t want to have such a cool car to look at each time they walk in the garage?


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)
